applyIt: Think of one area where you feel short of something right now, whether time, rest, money or patience. Take a quiet minute to name it, then say the first line of the verse slowly, as a way of placing that need in the care of the one it calls a shepherd. You do not need to feel certain or calm first. The verse simply invites you to start from trust.

citations.source: STEP Bible, TAHOT (Translators Amalgamated Hebrew OT), Tyndale House Cambridge

didYouKnow: The verb 'echsar is the word for being short of something, and it sits directly after lo', the word for not. Together they form one negative statement that nothing is missing.
historicalContext: The heading attributes this psalm to David, though whether the headings are original is debated. The psalm is well known, and its first line sets the tone for what follows: a series of pictures of rest, guidance, protection and provision. The verse makes its claim of trust before any details are given. Psalms like this one were used in worship and in personal prayer.
lifeInBibleTimes: Shepherding was a common part of life in the ancient Near East, and many people would have known flocks firsthand. A shepherd probably led the sheep to grass and water, knew each animal, and kept watch over the flock. The word used here for shepherd is the ordinary everyday word, so the picture would have been familiar to people who lived near herds and flocks. Being compared to a sheep meant depending on someone who knew the way and kept watch.
meaning: The verse opens with a simple picture. God is compared to a shepherd, and the speaker calls him 'my shepherd', which makes the picture personal. A shepherd looks after sheep by leading them, feeding them and keeping them safe. The second half says 'I shall lack nothing', meaning that the one who trusts this shepherd will not be left in need. The verse is a statement of trust, and the rest of the psalm shows what that trust looks like in practice, as the shepherd leads through green pastures, beside still waters and even through dark valleys.
theology: The verse says that God cares for his people and that they can rest in that care. The name here is Yahweh, the personal name of God, which English Bibles usually print as LORD in capital letters. Jesus later uses the shepherd picture of himself in John 10, describing himself as a shepherd who knows his sheep. Isaiah 40:11 pictures God gathering and carrying his flock, and Philippians 4:19 speaks of God supplying what his people need. Trust in this shepherd is what the verse invites.
